Scup (Stenotomus chrysops) is a commercially important sparid fish inhabiting the coastal waters of the northwestern Atlantic, where it supports both recreational and commercial fisheries. During a research survey conducted in southern New England, gravid female Scup were collected and their reproductive condition was assessed through gonadal biopsies. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 4.5% [GSI = 4.5%] for fish maintained at 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C]. Histological examination of the ovarian tissue confirmed the presence of vitellogenic oocytes in all individuals sampled. This gonadal condition aligns with the species' extended summer spawning period, during which multiple batches of pelagic eggs are released into the water column over several weeks.

The life history trajectory of Scup is characterized by a relatively rapid progression through early stages before reaching a pronounced asymptotic size. Field sampling across the species' range indicates that the ultimate total length attained by older adults is roughly 46 cm [Li = roughly 46 cm], a value derived from the upper tail of the length-frequency distribution of trawl-collected fish from Georges Bank. Individuals reach the total length at puberty, approximately 15.5 cm [Lp = approximately 15.5 cm], typically within their second or third growing season, after which reproductive activity commences. This length at first maturation is notably smaller than the maximum reported size, indicating a substantial post-maturity growth phase during which energy is partitioned between somatic increase and gamete production. Comparative data from congeneric sparids suggest that the length-based maturation schedule is influenced by local population density and thermal regime.

Reproductive output in Scup is closely tied to female body size, with larger females contributing disproportionately to the egg pool. At length at puberty, a female weighing approximately 68.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 68.4 grams] wet weight would produce relatively few eggs per spawning event. In contrast, a fully grown female achieving the asymptotic wet weight of 1826 grams [Wwi = 1826 grams] can produce tens of thousands of pelagic eggs per batch, with batch fecundity scaling as a power function of body mass. This substantial fecundity at the upper end of the size range is a common feature among iteroparous marine fishes, where lifetime reproductive output is maximized by repeated spawning over many years. The energetic investment in egg production is partially offset by the relatively low wet weight at birth of the larvae, with newly hatched individuals emerging at only 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams].

Embryonic and early larval development in Scup proceeds rapidly under the warm summer temperatures typical of its inshore nursery habitats. At a stable water temperature of 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C], the age at birth, defined as the time elapsed from fertilization to chorion rupture and the emergence of the yolk-sac larva, is approximately 6.5 days [ab = approximately 6.5 days]. This rapid eclosion is consistent with the developmental rates documented for other sparid fishes with pelagic eggs, where elevated temperatures accelerate enzymatic processes including chorionase secretion. Following hatching, the lecithotrophic larva relies on its endogenous yolk reserves for nourishment during a brief endotrophic phase before mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding. The timing of this trophic switch is critical for larval survival, as the larvae reach the point of no return if first feeding is delayed beyond the resorption of the yolk sac.

Longevity estimates for Scup based on otolith annulus readings from the Mid-Atlantic Bight indicate that the oldest individuals documented in the wild attain a lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] under the prevailing thermal conditions at 23.5 °C [T = 23.5 °C]. This lifespan is intermediate among northwestern Atlantic sparids, falling between the shorter-lived species such as Stenotomus caprinus and the more long-lived porgies of the genus Pagrus. The annual mortality rate declines substantially after the first few years of life, with the majority of the adult population consisting of fish aged 3 to 7 years. The ten-year maximum longevity translates into a generation time of roughly 4 to 5 years, allowing for multiple reproductive seasons over the course of a lifetime. Because Scup exhibit indeterminate growth, body size continues to increase gradually even in advanced age, contributing to the high fecundity observed in the largest females.
